papers.title: Evidence for a Collective Intelligence Factor in the Performance of Human Groups
papers.finding: Two studies with 699 people found a shared factor in small groups’ performance across tasks, associated with social sensitivity and conversational turn-taking.
papers.limit: These associations do not show that equal speaking time causes better decisions, or measure democratic legitimacy.

papers.title: How social influence can undermine the wisdom of crowd effect
papers.finding: In numerical estimation tasks with 144 participants, seeing others’ estimates reduced diversity and increased confidence without a corresponding improvement in collective accuracy.
papers.limit: An estimation experiment is not a general verdict against discussion; task and interaction structure matter.

papers.title: Fair algorithms for selecting citizens’ assemblies
papers.finding: Optimizes selection probabilities among volunteers while meeting demographic quotas; evaluates fairness on data from ten assemblies.
papers.limit: Fairness within the volunteer pool does not solve unequal willingness or ability to volunteer.

papers.title: Polis: Scaling Deliberation by Mapping High Dimensional Opinion Spaces
papers.finding: Describes a system that maps agreement patterns and surfaces statements supported across opinion groups, with real consultation cases.
papers.limit: A useful map of participants is not a representative estimate of an entire population or evidence that consensus is always desirable.

papers.title: Proportional Participatory Budgeting with Additive Utilities
papers.finding: Develops proportionality axioms and allocation rules for projects with different costs and additive utilities; a foundation for the Method of Equal Shares.
papers.limit: A guarantee depends on its preference model and precise axiom. It does not make every outcome fair under every definition.

papers.title: AI can help humans find common ground in democratic deliberation
papers.finding: The Habermas Machine uses opinions and critiques to revise group statements. Across experiments with 5,734 participants, AI statements were preferred to those from human mediators.
papers.limit: Preference for a statement is not proof of factual accuracy, legitimate authority, or lasting political agreement.

papers.authors: Yang, Hausladen, Peters, Pournaras, Hänggli Fricker & Helbing
papers.title: Designing Digital Voting Systems for Citizens: Achieving Fairness and Legitimacy in Participatory Budgeting
papers.finding: Studies how voting-system design shapes citizens’ perceptions of fairness and legitimacy in participatory budgeting.
papers.limit: Perceived fairness and actual understanding are different outcomes; evaluate them separately.

papers.title: Synthetic Replacements for Human Survey Data? The Perils of Large Language Models
papers.finding: Synthetic responses could match survey averages while understating variation and changing statistical relationships. Results were sensitive to prompts and collection dates.
papers.limit: The study tests particular models and tasks; use its evaluation questions rather than assuming identical failures for every later model.

papers.title: A General Theory of Proportionality with Additive Utilities
papers.finding: Proposes proportional rules for scored preferences under general feasibility constraints, and proportional rankings.
papers.limit: A theoretical proposal, not a deployment evaluation. Constraints and the definition of proportionality must be specified.

papers.title: LLM Agents Grounded in Self-Reports Enable General-Purpose Simulation of Individuals
papers.status: Preprint · June 2026 revision of a 2024 paper
papers.finding: Builds agents from interviews and/or surveys of 1,052 Americans and evaluates predictions on held-out responses against people’s own test–retest consistency.
papers.limit: Predictive fidelity on studied tasks does not confer consent or political authority. The earlier title was Generative Agent Simulations of 1,000 People.

papers.title: Komitee Equal Shares: A Hybrid Algorithm for Priceable Participatory Funding
papers.status: Published conference extended abstract · field deployment
papers.finding: Combines personal preferences with group evaluations and allocation receipts. In Winterthur in 2025, 38 citizens allocated CHF 380,000 to 43 projects.
papers.limit: One deployment, with 32 survey respondents. Simulated comparisons do not isolate every component’s causal contribution.

papers.title: Belief Engine: Configurable and Inspectable Stance Dynamics in Multi-Agent LLM Deliberation
papers.finding: Maintains explicit proposition-level stances with configurable evidence uptake and prior anchoring, recording the evidence associated with updates.
papers.limit: Evidence scoring and update rules are modeling choices. An inspectable trace is not by itself a faithful simulation of a citizen.

papers.title: Fairness and Abstraction in Sociotechnical Systems
papers.finding: Explains how isolating a technical model from its social setting can undermine fairness goals.
papers.limit: A conceptual analysis of system design, not an empirical guarantee that a particular civic tool is fair.

papers.title: Generative Social Choice: The Next Generation
papers.finding: Selects representative statements under a text-length budget, combining social choice with LLM queries.
papers.limit: Representation guarantees depend on the preference model and query assumptions; this does not certify every summary as fair.

fields.description: How can discussion include different views and inform public decisions?

contexts.name: Swiss direct democracy
contexts.process: A federal popular initiative proposes a constitutional change; an optional referendum challenges legislation.
contexts.problem: A voter or organizer needs to understand the text and the published procedural status.
contexts.build: A comparison of the proposal with the status quo, or a tracker using official records.
contexts.test: Can a reader find the relevant passage and explain what is being proposed?

contexts.name: ETH student representation
contexts.process: Fachvereine and VSETH represent students in departmental and ETH-wide bodies; VSETH’s members’ council governs its own budget, elections and statutes.
contexts.problem: A student needs to identify who can act and what has already been discussed.
contexts.build: An agenda brief or issue record connecting a concern, evidence, the responsible body and its response.
contexts.test: Can another student identify the responsible body and the present status?

contexts.name: Citizens’ assemblies and consultations
contexts.process: Participants examine evidence, discuss alternatives and produce recommendations or consultation outputs.
contexts.problem: An important concern can disappear when discussions are summarized.
contexts.build: A source-linked correction or unresolved-question record.
contexts.test: Compare the account with original contributions; count unsupported claims and missing requirements.

contexts.name: Participatory budgeting
contexts.process: Develop proposals, assess feasibility and allocate a limited budget using a defined procedure.
contexts.problem: A proposer needs to meet requirements; a participant needs to understand how the allocation was produced.
contexts.build: A feasibility checklist, comparison of rules, or readable allocation receipt.
contexts.test: Hold ballots and costs fixed for a rule comparison; ask a participant to explain an allocation.

contexts.name: Accountability after a decision
contexts.process: Connect an adopted proposal to responsibility, implementation and public reporting.
contexts.problem: A resident can see that a proposal was approved but cannot tell what happened next.
contexts.build: A proposal-to-implementation record using existing milestones and evidence.
contexts.test: Can a reader identify the current status, responsible body and supporting record?

history.analogy: Institutional rules can be inspected, borrowed and revised; political change requires legitimacy and is not automatically improvement.

sources.label: US Senate
sources.claim: The 1787 constitutional compromise combined a House apportioned by population with two senators per state.

sources.label: Swiss Parliament: 1848
sources.claim: The 1848 Swiss Constitution established a bicameral federal parliament, using the United States as a model.

sources.label: Australian Parliament
sources.claim: Australia combines parliamentary government responsible to the elected house, drawn from Westminster, with a federal Senate inspired by the United States.

sources.label: Australian Constitution
sources.claim: The Australian Constitution took effect with federation on 1 January 1901.

sources.label: UK Parliament
sources.claim: The Parliament Acts of 1911 and 1949 permit certain public bills to pass without Lords consent. The 1949 Act reduced the delay for eligible non-money bills from two years to one. Money bills and other categories have different provisions; the Lords did not lose every veto.

sources.label: Swiss Parliament: referendums
sources.claim: The optional federal legislative referendum dates to 1874. The mandatory constitutional referendum already existed in 1848.

sources.label: Swiss Parliament: initiatives
sources.claim: The federal popular initiative for partial constitutional revision dates to 1891. The initiative for total revision predates this, going back to 1848.

sources.label: Australian Electoral Commission
sources.claim: Preferential voting for the House of Representatives was introduced in 1918; compulsory voting at federal elections in 1924. Senate proportional representation was enacted in 1948 and first used in 1949, not at federation in 1901.

sources.label: Swiss Federal Archives
sources.claim: Political participation was historically restricted. Swiss women gained federal voting rights in 1971.

sources.label: US Senate: British and state precedents
sources.claim: The US framers drew on British institutions and state constitutions. The connection represents selected institutional precedents, not a literal fork of modern Westminster government.

sources.label: Swiss Parliament: proportional National Council elections
sources.claim: Proportional election of the National Council was approved in 1918 and first used in 1919.

history.diagram: One schematic branching lineage combines selected influences and dated reforms. Dates are labels, not a proportional horizontal time scale.
